Every Thursday at 3:12, Mara finds it in the bread rack. Same book always: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, stamp from a library forty miles away. She'll put it on the flour bin, wipe butter off the cover, and mean to return it after her shift. By noon, the heat and errands and sleep do it. Next Thursday, there it is again, wedged between the cooling rye loaves.

Tonight the bakery hums: proofing cabinet, old radio static. Rain draws silver lines down the front window. Mara picks up the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.

A folded receipt marks the heron chapter.

She opens it. In block letters: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.

She turns to page 47. A grey heron in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Pencil under the picture: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicks once.

She brushes flour off her apron, unlocks the front door, and flicks on the little OPEN sign.

She turns to 47. Grey heron in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under it, in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30? The clock over the mixer clicks once. She brushes flour off her apron, unlocks the front door, and turns on the little OPEN sign.

Every Thursday at 3:12, Mara would find that book in the bread rack. Always the same book, Practical Guide to Inland Birds, with the spine cracked, blue, and the library stamp from a town forty miles away. She would put it on the flour bin and wipe butter off the cover. Meant to return it after her shift. But by noon, errands, heat and sleep, the thought disappeared. Then next Thursday there it was again, tucked between cooling rye loaves.

Tonight, the bakery hummed with the proofing cabinet and the old radio's static, rain made silver lines on the front window. Mara lifted the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.

A folded receipt marked the chapter on herons. She opened it. In block letters, somebody had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. Page 47.

Mara turned to page 47. A grey heron stood in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under the picture, in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicked once. Mara brushed flour off her apron, unlocked the front door and turned on the little OPEN sign.

So magical, so awe-inspiring. It’s about lost love. She finds love at the beginning, then it’s gone. And the plot goes through twists and turns I didn’t expect. The lighting, the water imagery, the music, the visual design, it all comes together beautifully, and there are some truly breathtaking moments. Actors, dancers, synchronized swimmers, acrobats, everyone together, and it’s so incredibly precise. You get these wild flips, dramatic dives into the water, the swimmers holding their breath for seconds at a time. And somehow it balances emotional drama with genuinely funny moments. I was completely swept up in it. It’s imaginative, grand, surprisingly moving. If you have the chance, go. A must-see.

So a simple rain gauge is pretty straightforward. You have a funnel catching precipitation and directing it into a cylindrical tube. The top opening is wider than the tube so you get accurate readings. This difference acts as an amplifier. If the collection opening is ten times the area of the inner tube, an inch of rainfall fills the tube to a height of ten inches. This is so small amounts like hundredths of an inch can be read easily and precisely. But these instruments do have error sources. One is evaporation. The water you catch will evaporate quickly, especially in warm or windy weather. Another big one is wind exposure. Strong winds make turbulence around the mouth of the gauge. This can carry raindrops over the opening, so the gauge actually underestimates how much it really rained.

A rain gauge is pretty simple. It's just a funnel catching rain. The top is wider than the inner measuring tube. That's the whole design. It's a magnification. If the top is ten times the area of the tube, one inch of rain falls in, it fills the tube ten inches high. And now you can read hundredths of an inch really easily and precisely. And then you can read very small amounts of rainfall. But you can introduce errors. Evaporation is one. It can evaporate pretty fast. And then you're not measuring the actual rainfall, you're measuring the rainfall that didn't evaporate. Then you have wind. Strong winds blowing around the mouth of the gauge. The turbulence means a lot of raindrops go over it. So you're underestimating.

So the rain gauge is pretty simple. Rain falls into a funnel and then into a cylinder. The top of the funnel is much bigger than the tube below. So if it is ten times the area, then an inch of rain will fill the tube up to ten inches. This magnification allows you to read it very easily and precisely. You can measure hundredths of an inch. But rain gauges are subject to some errors. One is evaporation. The rain that collects in the gauge can evaporate quickly, especially in warm or windy weather. Another is wind exposure. If there is a lot of wind blowing, it creates turbulence around the mouth of the gauge. And that can carry rain drops over the mouth, and so it will underestimate the rainfall.

I'm not going to lie to you. The ovens hummed their low lullaby. Yeast, burnt sugar. I wiped flour off my forearms, checked the clock. 3:17 AM. Thursday. The bookstore was dead. No customers. I walked to the front counter and found a paperback sitting on the glass display case. The Shadow of the Wind. It had been there six weeks. Every night I'd toss it in the return bin, assume some confused person left it in the bakery's late-night drop slot thinking it was a library return. But tonight it was different. The book was warm, not the cool air of the shop. Picked it up. Opened it to the bookmarked page. A folded square of notebook paper fell out. Unfolded. Jagged, hurried writing. I know you're reading it. Keep going. Page 204 changes everything. Heart pounding, hammering against my ribs. Sharp rhythm against the quiet hum of the mixers. Looked around the empty shop. Shadows stretched long across the tiled floor. Nobody there. Back to the note. Back to the book. Trembling fingers, turned to 204. Text blurred. Closed the book, pressed it flat against the counter. Reached for my pen.

The ovens were making that low, constant hum. It was 3:17 on Thursday morning, and the air was dense with the smell of yeast and burnt sugar. I wiped flour off my forearms and went to the front counter. Under the glass display case, the same old paperback had been sitting for six weeks now. It was called The Shadow of the Wind. I picked it up. The pages were worn, dog-eared, and felt oddly warmer than the cool air. Normally I’d just toss it in the return bin next to the register, figuring some confused customer had left it. But tonight was different. I opened it to the bookmarked page and a folded square of lined notebook paper fell out and landed on the counter. I hesitated, then opened it up. The handwriting was jagged, hurried, like somebody wrote it in a rush. It said: I know you’re reading it. Keep going. Page 204 changes everything. My heart was hammering against my ribs, a sharp rhythm that cut through the quiet hum of the mixers. I looked around the empty shop, shadows stretched long across the tiled floor. Nobody was there. I looked back at the note, then at the book. My fingers were trembling. I turned to page 204. The text blurred before my eyes. I closed the book, pressed it flat against the counter and reached for my pen.

The ovens were humming their low steady hum. It was Thursday, 3:17 AM. He wiped flour from his forearms. He walked to the front counter. It was just as it had been for the past six weeks. On the glass display case sat a single worn paperback. It was The Shadow of the Wind. He picked it up, feeling its familiar weight, its dog-eared pages. It was slightly warmer than the air in the shop. Usually he would have put it in the bin, thinking a confused customer had mistaken the bakery's drop-box slot for a library return. But tonight, something felt different. He opened the book to the bookmarked page. A square of notebook paper slipped out and fluttered to the counter. He unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, hurried. The note said, "I know you're reading it. Keep going. Page 204 changes everything." His heart hammered against his ribs. Sharp sudden rhythm against the quiet hum of the mixers. The shop was empty. Shadows stretched long across the tiled floor. He looked back at the note, then the book. With trembling fingers, he turned to page 204. The text blurred before his eyes. He closed the book, pressed it flat against the counter, and reached for his pen.

I'm working with an orders table with about 120,000 rows and customers with about 9,000 rows. I want to add customer info to each order, so I merged them on customer_id using a left join.

But it's a bit off. If each order has only one customer, I expect 120,000 rows. So what I expected is 120k rows but it gives me 127k rows.

There are duplicate rows. So for example, when I check order 12345, I see two identical rows.

What I did was first check unique customer_id in orders - 9000, and in customers - 8750. So in customers I see some customer_ids are not unique. That is probably the issue.
And I checked the data types are both int64, so no type mismatch.

So the question is - how to make sure that each order is associated with only one customer, and how to figure out what causes the duplicate rows?

I'm getting duplicate rows when merging my orders and customers dataframes. Orders is 120k rows, customers is 9k. I'm using a left merge on customer_id. Merged ends up with 127,845 rows. I was expecting 120k, one customer per order. But clearly some orders repeat. E.g. order 12345 shows up twice. So I checked unique counts. Orders has 9000 unique customer_ids, customers has 8750. That explains it. Not every customer_id in orders is in customers, but that just makes some left merges become nulls. But the issue here is that the customers table is not unique on customer_id. If I check nunique on customer_id it's 8750, less than the 9000 rows, which means there are duplicate customer_ids. It's a data quality problem. That's what causes the expansion, and that's why I get 127k instead of 120k. So my next step is to dedupe the customers table. Either use drop_duplicates or drop_duplicates on customer_id. And then remeasure the result.

I've got a data frame with 120k orders, 8 columns, and a customers data frame with 9k rows and 5 columns. So I want to merge the customer information into the orders using the customer_id. What I was expecting was a 120k result, because each order has just one customer max. But if I merge, I get 127k, with some order id's repeated. For example if I check order id 12345, I get two rows, and they're the same. I checked the unique customer ids. The order has 9k unique customer ids, and the customer data frame has 8,750. So that's 250 missing customers. But all the customer ids are int64, and the data types are the same. But for some reason, when I merge, I get duplicates. How do I figure out what is causing the extra rows when I merge?

Three seventeen. The bakery smelled like yeast and silence. Marisol slid the first batch of bread into the oven and noticed it again. In the wicker basket by the back door. The Borrowers, well worn. Every Thursday for six weeks, someone would leave it there instead of the library two blocks over. No name. No card. Just the book, smelling faintly of rain and woodsmoke. Tonight a folded note was tucked between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her floury hands and opened it. I can't make it to the library before closing. Please keep it another week. I like knowing it's warm. She looked at the basket, then at the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing. Wrapped it in wax paper, tucked the note back into the book, and set both by the door. Then she flipped the sign to OPEN and started the coffee.

It was 3:17 a.m. in Marisol's bakery. It was quiet and there was the smell of yeast in the air. She was sliding the first loaves into the oven and she found the book again. The Borrowers in a wicker basket by the back door. She had been seeing this book every Thursday for six weeks now. No one was returning it to the library two blocks over. It was always returned here. There was no name, no card, just the book. It smelled faintly of rain and wood smoke.

Tonight, tucked between pages 84 and 85, was a folded note. She wiped off her floury hands and opened it. It said, "I can't make it to the library before closing. Please keep it another week. I like knowing it's warm." She looked at the basket and the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing, wrapped it in wax paper, tucked the note back into the book, and set both by the door. Then she flipped the sign to open and started the coffee.
